title: Colleges Embrace Streaming to Advertise Strengths
summary:
Colleges Embrace Streaming to Advertise Strengths
Johanna Alonso Wed, 10/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

With about 50 percent of TV viewership coming from streaming, colleges are turning to platforms like Netflix in hopes of getting prospective students’ attention.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
“History doesn’t happen quietly.”

So began a commercial for Sweet Briar College, a small women’s institution in Virginia, that aired on TV and video streaming services during the 2024–25 admission cycle. The 30-second ad featured shots of students dancing onstage, working in labs and riding horses, as well as a sweeping vista of the campus. It encouraged students to apply, emphasizing that only 225 first-year spots were available.

That rallying call seemed to work; the ad, which was targeted at Virginia households with 16- to 18-year-olds—as well as those with an interest in horses, given the college’s storied equestrian program—preceded a robust recruitment season. After it aired, applications increased 14 percent and deposits rose 22 percent, according to AmbioEdu, the marketing firm behind the campaign.

Christopher Smith, vice president of enrollment management at Sweet Briar, said he was inspired to add streaming and television to the college’s recruitment repertoire to enhance brand awareness and meet students and families where they are.

“For years, colleges have relied on traditional recruitment methods such as college fairs, high school visits, direct mail, you name it. These approaches really remain important, but we cannot assume that every student or family we want to connect with is hearing or seeing that message,” he said. “There are talented young women across the country who I feel would thrive at Sweet Briar but may not even know that we exist. [These ads] really provided another way for us to introduce those students and their families to opportunities available here.”

Sweet Briar isn’t the only institution turning to good, old-fashioned commercials as part of their marketing and recruitment campaigns. Jennifer Lonchar, co-founder of AmbioEdu, which specializes in TV and streaming advertisements for higher education, said that an increasing number of institutions are especially turning toward advertising on streaming as a new platform for attracting prospective students.

“Higher ed is always a hundred steps behind, I like to say, the ‘real world’ when it comes to marketing, and it always takes us a lot longer to adopt things,” she said. “Streaming is one of the fastest-growing spaces out there. It’s where a lot of marketers are moving their money. It’s not like it’s anything new; it’s been around for a while, but I think for higher ed, it has been something that has been slower to be adopted.”

Nielsen data shows that streaming is rising in popularity, making up about half of all TV consumption, and YouTube is the most popular streaming site.

Streaming also addresses one of the challenges colleges have faced when running TV commercials: measuring return on investment. AmbioEdu can track viewers who saw their clients’ ads on streaming to tell if they clicked through the ad and, eventually, if they submitted an application and enrolled. Having that data is important to institutions, which often need to prove a commercial can lead to real enrollment increases to justify the cost.

David A. Schweidel, a marketing professor at Emory University, told Inside Higher Ed that colleges might be turning to this type of advertising in part to combat demographic changes and concerns about the value of a degree.

One of the key purposes of advertising, he said, is to build trust and awareness of not only specific brands but also the type of product they offer.

“There are a lot of headwinds that higher ed is facing at the moment, and so I think that’s part of why you’re seeing the increased use of television advertising to get in front of people,” he said.

A college might want to invest in that type of advertising for a number of reasons, Lonchar said. For one, viewers are usually a captive audience; unless they pay for ad-free tiers, they typically must sit through a 30-second ad to continue their programming, in contrast with social media users who can just swipe past. Seeing the ads on well-known and respected platforms like HBO Max or Hulu can also give them some cachet, she said.

“I joke around with people and say it’s weird voodoo magic,” she said. “But really, when you think about it, it’s the power of TV that has existed for as long as TV has been around. We all grew up with commercials. We grew up watching things on TV and seeing brands over and over again. And that’s what this is.”

Leaders at Mission, an advertising agency in Baltimore that has run ad campaigns for local colleges and universities, said the main goal of a TV or streaming campaign is often to open the recruitment funnel—to make students aware of an institution they might not have heard of rather than push them to actually apply.

Once a student has seen the commercial, said Suzanne Rothrock, a principal at Mission, they might be retargeted via a social media ad, for example, which will hopefully encourage them to take a next step, like visiting campus.

“If they’re making that initial list of colleges, how can we reach them? How can they get them interested in a particular brand?” said Mike Eger, also a principal at Mission. “Maybe they’ve heard of this particular school, but they haven’t really considered it, but then, you know, they see a brand video and it gets them interested and then they start the search.”

Schweidel noted that marketing research indicates that even as streaming grows in popularity, TV and streaming are more commonly utilized by adults older than the Gen Zers currently entering college, who spend more time on social media apps like TikTok and Instagram. That means it might be better for ads on streaming to appeal to the parents of prospective students rather than the students themselves.

Lonchar said she’s received great feedback from institutions that say her company’s commercials have made a significant difference in application numbers and yield rates.

Such ads are “not a silver bullet,” she noted, but they do give institutions a unique way to interact with prospective students.

“We have never had an opportunity like this where we are essentially alone in the living room with the student and the parents, potentially, or the siblings. And I always tell my clients, ‘Think of it like this. If a student gave you 30 seconds and said, sell me on your school, what would you say to them?’” she said.

title: 4 Lessons on What Makes a College Degree Worthwhile
summary:
4 Lessons on What Makes a College Degree Worthwhile
Joshua.Bay Wed, 10/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

Recent research and initiatives highlight how students and institutions weigh the value of higher education beyond financial returns.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
What makes a college degree worth the investment? For students and families evaluating the costs and benefits of higher education, the answer may depend on more than tuition prices, future earnings or career prospects.

Recent research suggests that students find value in their college experiences in ways that extend beyond financial returns, even as questions persist about affordability and whether earning a degree delivers on its economic promise. Meanwhile, higher education leaders are working to strengthen student outcomes and demonstrate the worth of their institutions.

Here are four lessons from Inside Higher Ed’s Student Success coverage on what makes a college degree worthwhile.

Value extends beyond earnings.

Students may assess the value of their college experience through a broader lens than financial returns and career preparation, according to a new report from Qualtrics and Buro Happold that finds personal growth, relationships and belonging among the qualities students value most.

Based on a spring 2026 survey of 1,007 U.S. college students, researchers found that 74.2 percent of respondents reported receiving high or exceptional value from the sense of purpose and personal growth they experienced in college, the highest among nine dimensions of the college experience. Economic return ranked lowest at 66.2 percent, even as concerns about college costs and career outcomes continue to dominate debates about the payoff of higher education.

For Elliot Felix, a partner at Buro Happold and co-author of the report, the findings highlight the importance of understanding what students hope to gain from their college experience beyond the classroom.

“If you think about college, it’s a time for students to find their place, their people and their purpose,” Felix said. “Students are looking for value, and at the same time, they don’t want to measure it purely in terms of dollars and cents.”

Financial returns aren’t guaranteed.

Roughly 43 million Americans have some college credits but no credential. Re-engaging these adults could expand economic opportunities, but new research suggests the financial benefits of completing a degree vary considerably for those who return to college.

A report from California Competes examines the return on investment of a college degree among adults who previously stopped out and later graduated. Drawing on interviews with 27 California adult learners, researchers explored the financial, personal and social benefits of completing a degree, as well as the costs associated with returning to college.

About half of the graduates interviewed saw their earnings increase within three years of completing their degree, particularly those who returned with clear career goals. One graduate went from earning $10 an hour as a cleaner at a nursing facility to more than $100,000 annually as a nurse. But graduates in rural communities described more limited financial gains because of fewer local job opportunities.

Emi Fujita-Conrads, a researcher at California Competes and author of the report, said the findings underscore the importance of earlier career advising and better information about regional labor markets.

“Adult learners really need clear and early career guidance,” Fujita-Conrads said. “Students are getting career guidance, but it often arrives too late to make informed choices.”

The true cost of college isn’t always clear.

As students and families increasingly question the value of higher education, understanding the full cost of earning a degree has become an important part of the affordability discussion.

Federal law requires colleges to include estimated housing, food, transportation and other living expenses in their published cost of attendance. These allowances help determine financial aid limits and underpin measures such as net price and unmet need, but new research suggests they can vary considerably among institutions.

A recent report from the Hildreth Institute compared published living-cost allowances at 5,235 colleges against consistent external benchmarks based on local housing, food, transportation and other expenses. Researchers found that colleges serving students in the same local markets often publish markedly different estimates, making it harder for students and families to compare college costs and assess affordability.

Bahar Akman Imboden, managing director at the Hildreth Institute, said inaccurate or inconsistent estimates can affect students’ access to financial aid and ability to cover essential expenses.

“Colleges aspire to appear affordable,” said Akman Imboden. “College affordability cannot just be measured on whether students perceive college to be affordable at the time of entry. It must also account for whether that student has the resources to persist and complete.”

Higher ed leaders must demonstrate value through action.

As colleges and universities face growing scrutiny over the value of a degree, higher education leaders are pushing back against skepticism, arguing that student success has long been an institutional priority, even if those efforts aren’t always visible to the public.

Against that backdrop, five higher education associations recently launched the National Student Success Project, an initiative that brings institutions together around five commitments to help students succeed both during and after college.

Supported by the Strada Education Foundation, the initiative has attracted more than 50 colleges and universities as initial participants. Its five commitments focus on delivering strong value for students’ investments, creating clear and affordable pathways to credentials, advancing academic excellence, strengthening career preparation, and fostering supportive campus communities.

Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, said the project isn’t intended to establish a universal definition of student success, but rather identify and address the barriers that prevent students from achieving it.

“What we’ve fashioned is an action plan, not around defining student success—that’s up to all of our campuses—but defining the things that stand in the way,” Mitchell said. “Those five commitments represent doorways that we need to open for students so that they can prosper and they can achieve success.”

title: Top Research Universities Spent Less on Lobbying Congress in Q3
summary:
Top Research Universities Spent Less on Lobbying Congress in Q3
Josh Moody Wed, 10/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

As Congress adjourned to campaign for the midterm elections, lobbying from major research universities declined slightly.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
Top research universities dialed down their federal lobbying efforts over the last several months.

An analysis of federal lobbying expenses at major research institutions found that Association of American Universities members spent less in July through September than either of the prior two quarters of 2026.

Altogether, those universities and systems that lobby on behalf of AAU members spent nearly $7 million. That total is likely lower than the actual expenses, since some did not meet legally mandated filing deadlines. Comparatively, they spent just under $8 million in the second quarter of the year.

That figure, which comes ahead of midterm elections next month, is the lowest amount that AAU members have spent on federal lobbying since Inside Higher Ed began tracking the data in early 2025. Some institutions noted that congressional recesses also fell during the third quarter, which accounts for part of the decline.

But many of the top spenders remain the same as in previous quarters.

Among AAU member institutions, Johns Hopkins University is tied with Yale University at the top spot after spending $340,000 on federal lobbying in the third quarter of this year. The university lobbied on multiple issues including changes to the federal student loan program, accreditation reform, various health-care priorities, federal research funding, immigration policy and more.

“Johns Hopkins continues to advocate for our mission of research, education, and patient care,” a university spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement to Inside Higher Ed.

Yale—which is locked in negotiations with the Trump administration after the Department of Justice alleged it violated a Supreme Court ban on the consideration of race in admissions—significantly increased its lobbying expenditures between quarters. The university spent $340,000 in the third quarter up from $240,000 the quarter before. However, Yale averaged $310,000 a quarter in lobbying expenditures last year, so Q3 reflects a return to typical spending levels. Yale lobbied on federal funding, grant management, international student visas and other issues.

“Yale’s policy priorities have been consistent across reporting periods, namely protecting the university’s core missions of teaching and research, and the expenditures reported in any single reporting period vary naturally due to a number of factors,” a spokesperson wrote by email. “Since last year, Yale has opened an office in Washington, D.C., as part of its work to communicate higher education’s impact to legislators on both sides of the aisle.”

While Inside Higher Ed tracks spending by AAU members to better understand how top research universities are engaging with lawmakers, the overall top spender for the quarter is outside the AAU.

The University of Phoenix led all individual institutions in federal lobbying, racking up $410,000 in expenses. Phoenix has spent nearly $1.3 million on federal lobbying so far this year and totaled $1.9 million in 2025. The university has led on total lobbying expenditures since Inside Higher Ed began tracking the data. Lobbying priorities for Phoenix in the third quarter included bills to improve student financial aid verification processes, student veteran benefits and artificial intelligence, among other topics.

Here’s a look at the top spenders on federal lobbying among AAU members in the third quarter. The list includes individual universities only, not systems that lobby for multiple institutions.

Some institutions trended up in Q3 while others spent less on lobbying compared to previous quarters.

The University of Pennsylvania had the steepest drop among all AAU members. Penn spent $100,000 on federal lobbying in the third quarter, down from $280,000 in the previous period. (Penn officials did not respond to a request for comment from Inside Higher Ed.)

Cornell University also cut lobbying expenditures. While the university spent $360,000 in the second quarter, that number fell to $220,000 in Q3. Cornell’s spending tends to fluctuate; the university spent $180,000 in the first quarter of 2026 and the same amount in the fourth quarter of last year.

According to a spokesperson, Cornell recently “expanded our engagement with policymakers and federal agencies to restore research funding and prevent regulatory changes that would harm our educational programs and land-grant mission.” They added that the second quarter increase “was driven by reimbursement of AAU-led federal lobbying efforts.”

The University of California system, which lobbies on behalf of its member institutions, which includes AAU and non-AAU members, also spent significantly less in Q3 compared to other quarters. The UC system spent $250,000 compared to $840,000 in Q2 and $740,000 in Q1.

UC officials noted that congressional recesses accounted for part of the fluctuation.

“The University of California regularly engages with federal policymakers on a variety of issues in service to our education, research, health care, and public service mission,” UC spokesperson Rachel Zaentz wrote in an emailed statement to Inside Higher Ed.

“This includes advocating for legislation, policies, and programs that improve people’s lives—whether through world-class education, research that addresses our nation’s most pressing scientific and technological challenges, or high-quality health care. The associated costs may vary from quarter to quarter based on a variety of factors, including the timing of congressional recesses.”

title: America's long history of gerrymandering and its role in this year's midterms
summary: Following partisan battles over political maps, nearly 35 million Americans will vote in congressional districts redrawn ahead of this year's midterms. As the nation marks its 250th anniversary, Judy Woodruff explores the origins of gerrymandering and why this centuries-old practice remains one of the most powerful tools in American politics. It's part of her series, Crossroads: America at 250.
full_text:
Geoff Bennett:

Nearly 35 million Americans will vote in congressional districts that were redrawn ahead of this year's midterms following partisan battles over political maps.

As the nation marks its 250th anniversary, our Judy Woodruff explores the origins of gerrymandering and why this centuries-old practice remains one of the most powerful tools in American politics. It's part of her ongoing series Crossroads: America at 250.

Judy Woodruff:

The items on these cards are rare political artifact, protected by Library of Congress curators who carefully brought them out of their Archives.

Woman:

What you're seeing today is a copy of the original Boston Gazette, where you see the actual first appearance of the gerrymander cartoon.

Judy Woodruff:

What year was this?

Woman:

And this was March 26, 1812.

Judy Woodruff:

1812.

At the time, Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry had approved redrawn districts in the state in a bid to keep his party in power. As the story goes, a newspaper editor saw a salamander in the map's outline, combined it with Gerry's name, and a new word entered the American political vocabulary, gerrymandering, or, as it became, gerrymandering.

Nick Seabrook, UNF:

This is, I would argue, probably the very first example of a viral meme in American politics. So it spread around The Federalist newspapers in the New England era, and then over the subsequent year it was reprinted in almost 100 newspapers across the country.

Woman:

It's depicted as this mythical salamander beast.

Judy Woodruff:

The library also has the wood blocks used to print this piece of history. More than two centuries later, gerrymandering is flourishing and playing out in state after state.

The latest round of mid-decade redistricting intensified last year when, at President Trump's request, Texas redrew its congressional maps to try to add five Republican seats. After that, other states entered the fight. California Governor Gavin Newsom called a special election to redistrict and pick up more Democratic seats.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA):

They want to rig these elections and they want the power that gerrymandering provides, because they know what Donald Trump knows. He's going to lose the midterms.

President Donald Trump:

The Democrats, or as I call, the Dumocrats, because they are dumb in so many ways, they have redistricted for years, and now we took our shot, and it looks like we're going to pick up a lot of seats.

Nick Seabrook:

The motive for gerrymandering is almost always power. It's a product of polarization, of Democrats and Republicans not just disagreeing, but actively hating each other. Negative partisanship is such an incredibly strong force in our politics today.

Judy Woodruff:

Nick Seabrook is the author of "One Person, One Vote: A Surprising History of Gerrymandering in America."

He says the practice of manipulating district lines to protect political power is actually older than Gerry. It began with George Burrington, a colonial governor of North Carolina in the 1730s.

Nick Seabrook:

His attempt to manipulate the districts of the colonial assembly was motivated by a desire to try and prevent the columnists themselves, who elected the lower house of that legislature, from pushing back on the taxes and fees that his administration was charging to try and expand the footprint of the North Carolina colony.

Judy Woodruff:

So he had a motive, or motives, for what he was trying to do.

Nick Seabrook:

He did, yes.

Judy Woodruff:

Does that qualify as redistricting or gerrymandering as we know it today, manipulating?

Nick Seabrook:

I would say this was certainly gerrymandering because there was no -- there was no legal obligation for him to make any changes to these districts. He approached it purely as an exercise in maximizing his own political power.

Judy Woodruff:

This year, that maximizing of political power has ended up with mid-decade redistricting in nine states, Texas, California, Utah, Ohio, Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, and North Carolina.

From the colonial days of George Burrington to today, North Carolina has been one of the most gerrymandered states in the country. When congressional maps are redrawn, they sometimes split communities right down the middle. That's the case in the small town here of Sharpsburg, North Carolina, where three counties come together.

I'm standing at the northernmost edge of the Third Congressional District, but if I take just a few steps across these railroad tracks, you will see I have moved into the First Congressional District. When Republican state lawmakers redrew these and other lines last year, they said they were trying to pick up one more Republican seat in Congress.

Several counties shifted from one district to another, changing the demographics of both, spreading out eligible Black voters and weakening their electoral power. The city of Wilson is one of the communities plucked out of the First District and placed in the Third. For the 50,000 people who live here, the question is, what will the switch mean for their voice in Congress?

Castonoble Hooks has lived in Wilson his entire life.

Castonoble Hooks, Wilson, North Carolina, Resident:

This is a traditional Black area, where most of the original Black residents still live.

Judy Woodruff:

He remembers the days of Jim Crow laws, when the town was segregated.

Castonoble Hooks:

What disenfranchisement taught us is that if you're not a part of the political process, you are left behind.

Judy Woodruff:

Today, Hooks is a regular fixture at the senior center where he teaches chess and encourages his neighbors to vote.

Castonoble Hooks:

I voted in every election since I have been 18. Does my vote count? I hope it did. But I'm going to keep voting.

Judy Woodruff:

Do you think this new district that you're in, this newly drawn district, represents Wilson, the way it's drawn.

Castonoble Hooks:

No, it dilutes our vote. It dilutes the Black vote. It puts us with a large number of white people, so much so that our vote is -- if all of us vote one way, it probably won't affect the outcome.

Brittany Hamm, Wilson, North Carolina, Resident:

And it feels like our votes are kind of being taken away. It feels like our voice isn't heard, and that's what disconnects and make people not even want to vote.

Judy Woodruff:

Thirty-six-year-old Brittany Hamm was born and raised in Wilson. She's raising three kids here and works to educate people about the political process.

RAYMOND SMITH JR. (D), North Carolina Congressional Candidate: What we have before us, we have a Congress right now with no backbone.

(APPLAUSE)

Judy Woodruff:

She's a community organizer and active in local politics.

Brittany Hamm:

As constituents or voters, we're supposed to choose who represents us. When they redistrict or they redraw these lines, they're picking the voters, instead of the voters picking them. And that's not fair to us, because Wilson didn't move, the needs didn't change, but yet you're moving us.

Nick Seabrook:

It's an unfortunate situation where we, as the people, we as citizens can find ourselves cut out of that fundamental democratic role of choosing our representatives in government.

Judy Woodruff:

Nick Seabrook says the consequences go beyond any one community. They go to the heart of democracy itself.

Nick Seabrook:

Because elections are our only voice, there's no way that we can that we can fix that when the election itself has been -- has been rigged against us.

Judy Woodruff:

Is it consistent with democracy?

Nick Seabrook:

I don't believe that it is. I don't believe that you can call yourself a healthy democracy when gerrymandering is as rampant as it is in the United States today.

Judy Woodruff:

Given all this, where does it leave the average voter, the ordinary voter?

Nick Seabrook:

It leaves the average voter in a situation where they can never be sure in their individual districts, in their individual state whether the deck has been stacked ahead of time.

I argue that it's not sufficient to place constraints on redistricting to prevent gerrymandering. The only way to effectively fix this is to just take that power away from the elected branches of government, because you leave the foxes in charge of the henhouse. It doesn't matter how many sternly worded letters you send them telling them not to eat the chickens. That's what it's in their nature to do.

Judy Woodruff:

For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Judy Woodruff in Wilson, North Carolina.

title: Election denial has gone mainstream in the U.S. What does that mean for the midterms?
full_text:
Early on a Wednesday morning in October, a dozen people gathered in a wood-panelled room in Barry County, Mich., to be trained as poll workers for the U.S. midterm elections.

During the three-hour session, they were taught how to operate a vote-tabulating machine, check photo IDs and process absentee ballots.

But before the session began, Sarah VanDenburg, the clerk in this rural county, thanked them for "helping preserve our democracy."

The 2026 midterms are taking place while an election denial movement, empowered by President Donald Trump, has spent months claiming these otherwise routine tasks are the source of rampant fraud.

And even though there is little evidence to support these claims, they’re being used as a pretext by election deniers — many now in positions of authority — to try to interfere in the voting process.

Trump himself has mused openly about invoking a national emergency measure to alter how votes are counted.

In Barry County, sheriff Dar Leaf has emerged as the loudest voice pushing conspiracies about how elections are run. For the past six years, he has been using his office to circulate claims that foreign nationals hacked voting machines in the county in 2020 to switch votes from Trump to Joe Biden.

More recently, Leaf has been trying to interrogate state election officials as part of a new investigation into claims Michigan’s voter rolls for the 2026 midterms are being deliberately inflated with non-citizens, even though studies have shown non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

"I have a duty to go out and investigate, and I'm not gonna back down," Leaf told CBC News during an interview at sheriff headquarters in Hastings, Mich.

VanDenburg says she tries to maintain a good working relationship with the sheriff, but his beliefs "can make things difficult."

I have a duty to investigate, sheriff says

Leaf is a prominent figure in the Constitutional Sheriffs and Peace Officers Association, which believes sheriffs have ultimate authority in their county and has encouraged its members to investigate unfounded voter-fraud theories.

"It's just getting the sheriffs woke up to what their duties are really supposed to be," Leaf said about the association.

With help from his own deputies, Leaf tried to seize several voting machines in the county in 2021 and 2022 to prove his theory, only to be rebuffed by a judge and prosecutor who determined his claims had no merit.

In an unprecedented move last year, another member of the group, California sheriff Chad Bianco, seized 650,000 ballots from the 2024 election to probe claims of irregularities. A court ruled the seizure unlawful and ordered the ballots returned.

But the prospect of ballots, or voting machines, being seized by pro-Trump officials has alarmed elections observers, who worry such manoeuvres could disrupt oversight and make it difficult to verify results.

Asked if he would consider seizing ballots, Leaf told CBC News, "I would have to have a good reason to seize them. We'd probably seize and then go get a court order."

When election deniers are in charge

For decades, the U.S. Department of Justice monitored local compliance with federal election laws. But under Trump, election deniers now occupy senior positions in the department, which has aggressively sought evidence to support the president’s claims of widespread voter fraud.

For instance, the department is battling 30 states for access to sensitive voter information as part of an effort to find evidence of non-citizen voting.

The FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have also been tasked with investigating voter fraud, even though most studies suggest it's a rare phenomenon.

Trump has used the premise of widespread voter fraud to justify his attempts to have the White House exert more control over elections and rewrite rules in his favour. Since returning to power, he has ordered the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting and pushed Congress to pass a voter ID law that would have made it harder for millions of Americans to vote.

But the Constitution gives states, not the president, authority over elections. And courts, so far, have upheld that principle.

Can Trump call a national emergency?

The failure of these efforts, combined with polls suggesting the Republican majorities in Congress are in jeopardy, has led some in the election denial movement to urge Trump to take even more drastic measures, such as calling a national emergency.

Proponents of the measure argue voting machines are so vulnerable to foreign hacking that an emergency would be warranted on national security grounds.

In an interview with Time magazine published earlier this month, Trump was asked about the possibility of declaring a state of emergency. "I don't rule anything out or in," he replied.

Lorenzo Sewell, a Detroit pastor with ties to the Trump administration and several Republicans in Congress, said calling a national emergency would allow the president to order states to stop using vote-tabulating machines and halt mail-in balloting.

"But in terms of getting something like this, he needs people. He needs another January 6th, and that's what I'm advocating for, minus the violence," said Sewell, who spoke at Trump’s second inauguration and the Republican convention this summer.

Many legal experts say the idea is unconstitutional and almost certain to be blocked by the courts.

"Our entire constitution is based on the idea that the president has no power over elections," said David Becker, a former elections lawyer with the Department of Justice who now heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

Training 'democracy defenders'

State lawmakers and progressive voting-rights groups are nevertheless preparing for a wide range of scenarios on election day, including the prospect of confrontations with armed federal agents or pro-Trump crowds.

"It seems the rhetoric has become more violent," said Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of Michigan United, a Detroit-based social justice organization that's been training "democracy defenders" in de-escalation tactics.

She recalled how, in 2020, a crowd of Trump supporters attempted to disrupt poll workers counting mail-in ballots in Detroit.

"That's why we have our democracy defenders," Butler said. "These are the scenarios that we're thinking about and planning for."

VanDenburg, the Barry County clerk, is hoping her preparations will help prevent tensions from boiling over on election day.

She recently gave a presentation to the sheriff and his deputies about basic election day rules, such as who can enter a polling station (armed officers are not allowed).

Leaf welcomed the information, saying, "some of those things we've never been taught before."

Those working the polls in the county will mostly be people from the community, which VanDenburg says will lighten the atmosphere.

"You walk into the polling place and you feel warmth. You feel invited, which I think is very important for our voters to feel that way."

title: UK unis to take £1,010m hit over international student levy
summary:
The UK's upcoming levy on international student fees will batter universities' bottom lines by £110 million more than previously anticipated, according to a new government impact assessment.

The post UK unis to take £1,010m hit over international student levy appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
In the first three years of the £925-per-international-student levy being applied, UK providers are expected to take a £1,010m hit in lost fees – significantly more than the government predicted just last year, when it estimated that they would lose out on £900m.

The policy is also expected to raise less money – earmarked to be spent on maintenance loans for domestic students – that previously thought, with projections suggesting that £1,340m will be levvied compard to the £1,390m predicted in a 2025 impact assessment.

An updated impact assessment on the policy landed this afternoon, on the same day HM Treasury snuck a line into its 2026 Budget that revealed it would extend the Graduate Route back up to two years for grads of “high-compliance universities” with strong labour market outcomes. Details of the policy remain unclear.

However, the new impact assessment tells a happier story about the number of international students the UK is expected to lose out on as a result of higher fees (with most instutions expected to pass on levy costs to students).

Some 11,500 fewer international students are expected to make their way to the UK in the levy’s first seven years, according to today’s impact assessment. This compares to a projected 16,500 students lost projected in 2025’s assessment – a differential of 5,000.

However, the government stressed that future international student numbers were “inherently uncertain”. “The international student market is competitive, and inflows to the UK depend on a range of factors, including recruitment strategies from international competitors, exchange rates and other economic variables,” it said.

In more worrying news for many of the UK’s higher education institutions, today’s impact assessment acknowledges that the levy will not affect all providers equally.

The international student market is competitive, and inflows to the UK depend on a range of factors

Department for Education

A two-tier system has emerged, where higher ranking universities are expected to be able to pass on a higher proportion of levy costs to their international students without seeing too much of a recruitment drop off compared to lower ranking institutions.

So-called Tier 1 (Oxford University, Cambridge University and Imperial College London) and Tier 2 (the remaining universities in the Complete University Guide’s top 20) are expected to fair better than lower-ranked (Tier 3 and 4) institutions – mirroring the expected effect of more stringent compliance measures universities must now adhere to.

Commenting on the news, director (education) at PF Global, Jess Lister, said the announcement was “timely as the sector is gearing up for another attempt to quash the levy”.

Lister noted that previous modelling from Public First had “junked the idea providers would be able to simply pass on all the costs as the Home Office was assuming”.

“Pleased to see how our very rapid turn around modelling is holding up 1.5 years later now the government has gotten around to doing its own analysis,” she said.

The levy has drawn serious criticism from the UK’s higher education sector, with detractors warning that policy makers were risking one of the UK’s most lucrative industries.

Artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape in ways traditional higher education cybersecurity models weren’t built to handle. A campus attack surface can be complex, with decentralized IT structures, sprawling networks, and a host of sensitive student and research data that is attractive to cybercriminals. AI is raising the stakes, giving bad actors the ability to launch sophisticated attacks with less effort than before, while also giving IT teams new tools to fight back.

“We should be concerned about the increasing ability of AI as a technology to discover and exploit weaknesses,” says Buck Bell, director of CDW’s Global Security Strategy Office. “It’s incumbent now on security practitioners to leverage similar tools to find those weaknesses before the bad guys find them. But we also need to be able to measure risk more broadly.”

In CDW’s 2026 Cybersecurity Research Report, organizations across industries shared how they’re working to fight AI-powered attacks with AI-backed solutions.

Click the banner below to read the full CDW Cybersecurity Research Report.

The Threats:

43% of respondents experienced AI-enhanced or AI-generated phishing attacks in the past year

37% faced AI-powered malware

Top concerns are AI-generated phishing and social engineering (25%) and AI-powered automated attack tools (21%)

The Response:

41% plan to deploy AI-driven threat detection and behavioral analytics

49% are already using AI for threat and anomaly detection

47% are using AI for threat intelligence analysis

28% are maximizing security spending through automation, integration and consolidation

The Gaps:

31% use quantitative financial modeling to assess business impact, suggesting most organizations measure cybersecurity through technical metrics

46% say complex IT and cloud environments are their biggest challenge in quantifying cybersecurity risk

26% say 24/7 threat monitoring ranks as their biggest operational struggle — the top response — driving demand for managed security services

Shift from reactive to proactive.

Reduce hidden waste by addressing scheduling rigidity.

Match the right room to the right pedagogy.

Protect expensive classroom technology with runtime discipline.

Deploy AI-powered physical security as operational intelligence.

Build a true partnership among IT, facilities and academic scheduling.

title: North Carolina’s Elite Colleges: Who’s Most Selective?
summary: University Learning Environment The nation’s medical research institutions and highly selective conservatories known for their rigorous audition and application processes likely come to mind first when you hear the term “elite schools in North Carolina.” But for our purposes, “elite” has a broader definition. full_text:
The nation’s medical research institutions and highly selective conservatories known for their rigorous audition and application processes likely come to mind first when you hear the term “elite schools in North Carolina.”

But for our purposes, “elite” has a broader definition. The North Carolina schools that made this list stand out for their research, student bodies, or specialized expertise in niche fields.

To make this list, we ranked the schools using a qualitative editorial prestige index. We gave first consideration to national recognition for academic or research output (a large research footprint or recognition for a particular specialty).

That was followed by selectivity of admissions, and then research and mentoring opportunities for undergrads. When it came down to it, we gave a slight edge to schools with broad-based strengths.

This is an editorial ranking, not an official ranking. Admissions figures reflect different reporting periods and do not necessarily compare a single incoming class. While many of the schools on this list enjoy international prestige, we’ve included some regional standouts as well.

Sources checked as of October 2026.

15

Meredith College

Builds Research Around Faculty Mentoring

Meredith College offers research as part of the curriculum, for credit, through its undergraduate research courses.

Students can begin working with faculty members early on and work their way up to more advanced, original research projects.1 Meredith also has an advising and coaching system called StrongPoints.

Through it, students identify their personal strengths and use them to guide their academic, extracurricular, financial, and career development.2 Meredith provides individual coaching to help students with consistent support and guidance.2 Be sure to ask about this when visiting.

Meredith College may have a regional reputation, but its focus on mentoring and student development sets it apart. Research is an important part of the college’s undergraduate offerings. Meredith focuses on the process of completing original work with a professor.1

14

UNC Asheville

Makes Original Research Part of College Life

Over 65 percent of UNC Asheville undergraduates complete original research projects, and the university helped found the National Conference on Undergraduate Research.3

Students receive faculty mentoring and research grants, and they present their work at conferences on and off campus and in a UNC Asheville journal.3 Asheville’s research focus fits with its Liberal Arts Core, which asks all students to develop strong skills in critical thinking, inquiry and communication, and to pursue learning across a variety of disciplines.4

That broad foundation can help you apply what you’ve learned in new ways and make connections among seemingly unrelated ideas and concepts. It can help you choose a career or professional path.

If you’re interested in digging into a research project, whether in the environment, history, the creative arts or some other field, ask to see examples of recent student work in your intended major. Ask how mentoring relationships are formed.

13

Appalachian State

Combines Honors Seminars With a Senior Project

Students interested in honors programs should look into the Honors College at Appalachian State University. Admission to App State and admission to the Honors College are two separate processes.

The Honors College provides students with an opportunity to explore challenging coursework through small interdisciplinary seminars and additional coursework.5

Students in the Honors College must complete an international education experience.5 They participate in an intellectual community within the larger Appalachian community. Honors students must also demonstrate advanced scholarship in their chosen field in a culminating senior project.5

These senior projects can take many forms, including a research project, a systematic review, a film, an exhibition or performance, a creative writing project, or a project developed in partnership with a community agency.6 Whatever project students choose to pursue, they must submit a written component that explains the project in relation to methods used in their discipline.6 The Honors College at Appalachian State provides motivated students with a challenging honors program and a meaningful senior project.

12

UNC Greensboro

Brings Students Into Research Early

UNCG embraces a teacher-scholar model where students can join creative and research projects early.7 The Undergraduate Research Fellows Program admits about 70 first-year students each year to an introductory course where they visit professors, labs and studios and learn how to identify research opportunities.8

While UNCG doesn’t have the same reputation for selectivity as other elite institutions, it emphasizes access to research, with more than 700 undergraduates participating in research each year.7

For students wondering how they can get involved in research as first-years, what they can contribute, or who they should email, the Undergraduate Research Fellows Program offers a way to ease into the process. It’s not just for the sciences—students study anything from music to art.8 It’s the accessibility of research and UNCG’s emphasis on active scholarship that set the school apart.

It’s a reminder that you don’t have to wait until you’re a senior to make meaningful contributions.

11

East Carolina University

Has Reached R1 Research Status

In 2025, Carnegie recognized East Carolina University as an R1 school, which reflects its very high research activity.9 In 2023, research expenditures at ECU totaled $67.1 million.9 This research spans numerous disciplines, from health to technology to education.

Being an R1 school doesn’t necessarily equate to being selective, however, nor does it guarantee research opportunities for every student.

ECU does offer programs, awards, and other support to encourage research, including faculty-mentored awards, research incorporated into certain classes, help finding a mentor, and opportunities to showcase research.10 These resources offer clear routes from taking classes to conducting research.

Interested in research at ECU? Browse research being conducted in your areas of interest and ask how you can get involved as an undergrad.

10

UNC Wilmington

Turns Coastal Science Into Hands-On Study

For students whose interests focus on marine science, hands-on opportunities to get out into field sites and work with faculty on research projects may be the top priority in choosing a school. That’s where UNC Wilmington stands out, earning its spot in our rankings on the strength of one academic identity.

At the heart of UNCW’s marine science program is the Center for Marine Science, which involves graduate and undergraduate students in research in marine biotechnology, aquaculture, and coastal monitoring.11 The marine biology degree program also offers undergrads the opportunity to get involved in research projects through honors work, directed independent research, internships, or research assistantships.12

Through the Center for Marine Science, UNCW undergrads studying the marine environment have access to research vessels, advanced scientific equipment and labs, a shellfish research facility, imaging facilities, and seawater labs, as well as local field sites.1112

9

UNC Charlotte

Combines R1 Research With Honors Study

UNC Charlotte earned its Carnegie R1 classification in February 2025.13 Its R1 status reflects its commitment to expanding its research program.

Honors students at UNC Charlotte benefit from research opportunities. Honors programs provide honors candidates with specialized instruction and undergraduate research experiences.14 Candidates must qualify and be accepted into these programs.14

Honors candidates should look into research opportunities on UNC Charlotte’s campus while touring, and get a sense of what it would take to get involved in a research group.

They should also familiarize themselves with honors requirements while visiting UNC Charlotte. Honors students must complete a thesis or special project, and earn candidacy by following specific steps.14

UNC Charlotte’s designation as an R1 school provides it with a foundation for future growth through grants and partnerships.

Combined with a rigorous honors program, UNC Charlotte offers its honors students challenging coursework, in-depth research and one-on-one mentorship.14

8

North Carolina A&T

Expands Engineering and Research Funding

Those looking for evidence of institutional investment in engineering would do well to pay attention to what’s happening at North Carolina A&T. The numbers indicate a growing research program.

Its aeronautical and astronautical engineering degree, announced in June 2025, suggests the school’s ambitions aren’t limited to the strength it already enjoys as the top producer of African American engineering graduates.15

The College of Engineering has industry and research ties.15 North Carolina A&T is pursuing, but has not yet received, R1 status, according to its August 2026 report.16 Faculty brought in $113.3 million in research funding during fiscal 2026.16

Research funding and research expenditures are not the same thing.

If engineering is your thing, check out particular degrees, curricula, project teams, areas of faculty interest, and opportunities for research participation.

7

Elon University

Connects Study Abroad, Research and Service

Elon Experiences is Elon University’s framework for supporting and encouraging experiential learning.

The program recognizes that experiences such as study abroad, internships, research, leadership and service aren’t just extracurricular activities or add-ons. They’re ways for students to integrate and apply the knowledge they’re gaining in the classroom.17

Research offerings include faculty-mentored research for course credit, grants and funding for research-related travel, a forum for students to present their research in the spring, and a summer research experience.18 Elon ranked No. 12 in the 2027 U.S. News ranking for undergraduate research and creative projects.18 The achievement gives Elon national recognition for its educational approach.

Co-curricular and extracurricular pursuits can be enriching and important components of a college education, but they may have more meaning when they’re integrated into a student’s broader academic experience. A student who completes an internship, studies abroad and conducts independent research has accomplished a lot. What’s more important is being able to articulate the ways in which these experiences are connected and how they relate to the student’s academic interests, intended career or area of inquiry.

If you’re the kind of student who wants a college experience that includes many types of learning, paying attention to the way in which Elon weaves those opportunities together could be an important factor in your decision.

6

UNC School of the Arts

Selects Students for Conservatory Training

UNCSA focuses on finding and accepting students with specialized training and talent in their field of study.

Students apply to the university with portfolios, auditions or interviews, the requirements of which vary depending on the conservatory and level of study.19 Undergraduate programs are offered in dance, design and production, drama, filmmaking, and music.19

Ranked the third best drama school in the world by The Hollywood Reporter in 2026, UNCSA’s School of Drama was the highest ranked public school on the list.20 This is an industry-specific ranking.

As a conservatory, UNCSA may be stronger in its areas of expertise than our overall ranking would suggest.

Make sure conservatory training sounds like a good fit for you. Research the faculty and courses of study to make sure the level of talent and work required suits your goals.

5

NC State

Pairs Competitive Admission With Applied Research

With research expenditures of $633 million reported in the 2024 chancellor’s report, 15 startups based on university research, and work spanning semiconductors to sustainable proteins to textiles innovation, NC State’s research activities have breadth and strength.22

That research strength helps propel NC State to fifth place on our list. With so many programs, students would be well advised to learn more about the university and decide if NC State might be a good fit.

Those who want to transform their scientific ideas into processes, products, or solutions might especially want to learn more.

How can undergraduates get involved in projects? What background, skills or courses are necessary? When can students get involved?

According to the institutional facts report, NC State had 47,791 first-year applicants and admitted 19,722 for fall 2026, for a calculated admission rate of about 41 percent.21 This reflects the admission rate for NC State as a whole, not for individual majors or departments.

4

Wake Forest

Combines Selective Admission With Faculty Contact

Wake Forest’s name carries weight, but its selectivity goes beyond reputation.

In September 2025, the university reported a 20.8 percent acceptance rate for its entering class, evidence of just how competitive admissions can be.23 Three in five class sections at Wake Forest have fewer than 20 students, creating an environment that encourages participation.23

Research opportunities aren’t limited to upper-level students, and more than 100 Wake Forest students take part in research each summer.24

Through the Undergraduate Research and Creative Activities Center, Wake Forest undergraduates work alongside faculty mentors on original research projects.24 Wake Forest’s relatively low acceptance rate and small classes can make it a challenging and rewarding choice for students.

When applying to Wake Forest, dig into the specifics of your intended major to see how these elements operate in practice. Pay attention to the resources within your specific area of study. Smaller class sizes and research initiatives can pave the way for deeper conversations with fellow students and meaningful, long-term collaborations with professors.

3

Davidson College

Puts Undergraduates Into Faculty Research

Davidson College’s selectivity is high: the Class of 2030 has an acceptance rate of 14.2 percent.25 But that’s not the only reason it’s ranked as one of North Carolina’s elite schools.

Davidson’s undergraduate research program has students participating in faculty-led research projects.

Over 60 percent of Davidson faculty publish work with undergraduate co-authors, reflecting the breadth of the Davidson research community.26 Students can take independent research courses, write theses, engage in other intensive collaborations with Davidson faculty, and land paid summer research positions on and off campus.26

Co-authorship with faculty indicates that student research is reaching an audience beyond Davidson. Davidson College offers an option for prospective students looking for an alternative to large research universities.

It’s highly selective, but its undergraduate research program shows that students shoulder real research responsibilities.

2

UNC-Chapel Hill

Links Broad Research With Undergraduate Support

UNC-Chapel Hill ranks No. 2 for breadth of research and systems for involving students in research.

According to a facts sheet released in December 2023, UNC had $1.36 billion in research expenditures in federal fiscal 2022.27 This isn’t necessarily reflective of UNC’s research expenditures in this year’s budget. Its research covered a wide variety of areas, including health and life sciences and social sciences.27

To get students involved in research, the Carolina academic catalog describes an Office for Undergraduate Research that provides a host of services and programs. These include research opportunity listings, summer research fellowships, travel awards, and a forum for presenting research.28

The catalog notes that more than 500 students present their research at UNC’s annual Celebration of Undergraduate Research.28

Research opportunities will vary by department, so it’s important to explore your options. UNC-Chapel Hill offers a large research operation and an array of advising, funding, and presentation opportunities to get you started.

1

Duke University

Combines Highly Selective Admission With Large-Scale Research

Duke’s position at the top of our list of the best universities in North Carolina reflects its combination of selectivity, research investment, and opportunities for undergraduate research.

In March 2026, Duke reported admitting 2,930 students from a pool of 61,935 applicants for the Class of 2030, equating to a preliminary acceptance rate of 4.7 percent.29 Final numbers may shift slightly based on waitlist activity, but Duke is highly selective.

Duke’s Office for Research and Innovation reported that Duke had $1.5 billion in research expenditures in fiscal 2024.30

Through the interdisciplinary research initiative known as Bass Connections, Duke undergraduates can work alongside faculty and experts on research projects and special courses and take part in summer research programs.31 These address some of today’s most pressing social issues.

While Duke’s selectivity, research expenditures, and opportunities for undergraduate research earn it first place on our list, students should consider whether Duke’s programs, research opportunities, challenging environment, and price tag are right for them.

title: Einfach mal machen: Wie die Universität Münster echte Alltagsprobleme mit KI lösen will
summary:
Künstliche Intelligenz verspricht ein Mehr an Effektivität und Effizienz. Dementsprechend wird im Hochschulkontext sehr viel über mögliche Potentiale gesprochen und über theoretische Anwendungsmöglichkeiten verhandelt. Patrick Thiemig beschreibt, wie man aus der theoretischen Diskussion zur praktischen Umsetzung kommt. Doch warum ist Erfahrung so wichtig?

The post Einfach mal machen: Wie die Universität Münster echte Alltagsprobleme mit KI lösen will appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
In meinen Gesprächen als Change Manager der Universität Münster mit Kolleginnen und Kollegen dreht sich das Thema generative KI oft um die möglichen Anwendungsfälle und Potentiale. Was mir dann aber immer wieder begegnet, ist dieses diffuse Gefühl, nicht zu wissen, wo man beginnen soll. Rahmenbedingungen in Form von Richtlinien und Strategien sind richtig und wichtig und wenn diese dann mit Erfahrungswerten verbunden werden können, wird eine praktische und zum Teil schon erprobte Vorgehensweise dem definierten Rahmenwerk das nötige Leben einhauchen.

Aus diesem Grund hatte ich die Idee, diese Erfahrungsgrundlage zu schaffen. Formalisierte Fortbildungen in Form von Prompting-Workshops, also der How-To-Approach und somit das Handwerk, sind an der Universität Münster bereits seit 2025 etabliert. Wir wollten zusätzlich aber echten Austausch der Lernenden untereinander ermöglichen und einen gesicherten Rahmen schaffen, um sich auszuprobieren. In diesem agieren mein Kollege, Christian Richter, und ich nicht als Dozierende, sondern als Lernbegleitungen.

Da wir Agenten es als eine Chance begreifen, KI in Arbeitsprozesse zu integrieren, haben wir uns entschieden, ein sehr stark auf Partizipation ausgerichtetes Format umzusetzen. Darin legen wir einen hohen Wert darauf, generative KI und die damit zusammenhängenden Implikationen erfahrbar zu machen.

Jetzt könnte man sich natürlich die Frage stellen, warum wir die Funktion nicht einfach nur freigeben, ein E-Learning erstellen und dann die Kolleginnen und Kollegen einfach loslegen lassen? Genau das tun wir, aber es gibt ebenfalls Interessierte, die die erste Hemmschwelle nicht überwinden. Sie wissen schlicht nicht, wo sie anfangen sollen, erahnen aber das Potential. Genau für diese Zielgruppe wurde das Format entwickelt. Dieses ist bewusst offen gestaltet, sodass Professor:innen neben Assistent:innen, Entwickler:innen und Verwaltungsangestellten sitzen. Uns war es wichtig, die unterschiedlichen Hochschulperspektiven zusammenzubringen und nicht nach Zielgruppen aufzuteilen.

Das Format ist dreigeteilt, damit die Arbeitsphase möglichst produktiv ist. In einem halbstündigen Vorbereitungstermin per Zoom erklären wir die Lernziele und definieren Begrifflichkeiten. Des Weiteren wird eine Vorlage vorgestellt, die die Lernenden vorab ausfüllen sollen. In der Vorlage – inspiriert am Canvas des HFD-Botcamps – wird das Problem beschrieben und was ein Agent zur Lösung beitragen könnte. Ebenfalls werden Metadaten, wie zum Beispiel Datenverantwortliche, BSI-Grundschutzeinschätzung oder Risikobewertung, abgefragt. Diese Informationen dienen meinem Kollegen und mir zur Einschätzung, ob überhaupt ein KI-Agent die Lösung und das Vorhaben grundsätzlich umsetzbar ist.

Der Experimentierraum ist für 20 Personen geöffnet, findet in Präsenz statt und dauert drei Stunden. Wir haben uns für Präsenz entschieden, weil wir eine kollegiale Arbeitsatmosphäre schaffen und echten Austausch untereinander ermöglichen wollen. Zu Beginn der Veranstaltung zeigen wir, wie ein KI-Agent konfiguriert wird. Danach erstellen die Lernenden ihre jeweiligen Prototypen. Wir begleiten den Vorgang, beantworten Fragen und beheben Fehler.

Der zweistündige Abschlusstermin per Zoom ist ungefähr zwei Wochen nach dem Experimentierraum und behandelt dann zwei zentrale Fragestellungen: Wie testet man die KI-Agenten gründlich durch und wie haben sich die Prototypen weiterentwickelt? Ich erläutere die Testfälle und zeige in einer Live-Demo typische Fehlerquellen. Danach präsentieren die Lernenden ihre Prototypen und berichten von ihren Erfahrungen. Das ist uns besonders wichtig, weil wir Wert darauf legen, dass eine dauerhafte und etablierte Lerngemeinschaft entsteht und man sich gegenseitig zu neuen Ideen inspiriert.

Jetzt haben wir viele Prototypen, aber wie geht es damit weiter? Uns war es von Anfang an wichtig, dass KI nicht als Selbstzweck genutzt wird, sondern dass aus den Prototypen ein echter Mehrwert entsteht. Es wird also im Nachhinein geprüft, welche KI-Agenten für die gesamte Universität geöffnet und welche weiterhin privat oder teamintern geteilt werden. Daher haben wir zusätzliche Nutzungsbedingungen für agentische KI im Rahmen von uniGPT entwickelt, die Verantwortlichkeiten festlegen, Zugriffsrechte und Autonomiegrade der Agenten regeln und benötigte Kompetenzen zur Entwicklung, aber auch zur Anwendung, definieren. Dieser Zusatz ist aktuell noch nicht verabschiedet.

Die wichtigste Funktion der zusätzlichen Nutzungsbedingungen ist es, ein Rahmenwerk für die Erstellung und den Einsatz von KI-Agenten festzulegen. Es werden daher technische Fragestellungen (Darf das Model Context Protocol lesend eingesetzt werden? Welche Systeme darf der Agent auslesen? Wer darf auf die Agenten zugreifen?) behandelt, sowie Rollen und Verantwortlichkeiten.

Wir unterscheiden fünf wesentliche Rollen für den Einsatz von KI-Agenten: Agenten-Designer:innen (Konfiguration der Agenten), Datenkurator:innen (inhaltlich verantwortliche Personen), Technik (Bereitstellung der Infrastruktur), Sicherheit und Compliance (Prüfung der Agenten auf IT-Sicherheit insbesondere Schnittstellen) und Qualitätskontrolle (Kriterienkatalog und Rahmen). Ebenfalls enthalten sind Ziele der Kompetenzentwicklung, hier vor allem AI Literacy und agentenspezifische Professionalitätsanforderungen. Weiterhin haben wir eine Deprovisionierungsstrategie entwickelt, inklusive Kill-Switch-Szenario, für den Fall, dass KI-Agenten nicht mehr eingesetzt werden sollen. Es handelt sich um eine Notfallstrategie, falls KI-Agenten, wie aktuell mehrfach in den Medien berichtet wird, deaktiviert werden müssen.

Die Veranstaltungen wurden sehr gut angenommen. Innerhalb von zwei Monaten haben wir vier Durchgänge gehabt und die Plätze waren sehr begehrt. Ein Großteil der Teilnehmenden findet über Netzwerkeffekte den Weg zu uns und das Interesse an weiteren Terminen ist ungebrochen.

Die wichtigste Erkenntnis für uns war, dass die Kolleginnen und Kollegen für konkrete Probleme sehr innovative Lösungsideen entwickeln. Wir haben über 30 verschiedene Anwendungsfälle von Chatbots bzw. KI-Agenten identifizieren können. Unser Ziel, die Probleme als Ausgangspunkt zu nutzen und nicht fertige KI-Agenten bereitzustellen, hat sich für uns sehr gut bewährt und die Anwendungsbreite hat uns selbst überrascht. Wir konnten die typische Falle vermeiden, eine Lösung zu präsentieren und erst danach nach einem passenden Problem zu suchen.

Die praxisnahen Anwendungsfälle ermöglichen es uns, jetzt das dazu passende Rahmenwerk zu entwickeln und auch andere Akteurinnen und Akteure der Universität vom Nutzen generativer KI zu überzeugen.

Wir haben zudem das Gefühl, einen großen Schritt in Richtung KI-Kompetenzentwicklung zu machen. Die Teilnehmenden lernen nicht nur die eigentliche Erstellung von KI-Agenten, sondern ebenfalls die Grenzen und die Bedingungen von generativer KI kennen. Zwei grundlegende Erkenntnisse der Lernenden möchte ich hier hervorheben. Die erste Erkenntnis ist, dass die eigentliche Konfiguration von KI-Agenten gar nicht so schwierig ist. Bis die erste Version des Prototyps läuft, vergeht im Durchschnitt eine halbe Stunde.

Durch das sich entwickelnde technische Grundverständnis verlieren die Teilnehmenden das diffuse Gefühl, welches KI aufgrund der technischen Komplexität (Stichwort Blackbox) mit sich bringt. Die zweite Erkenntnis in diesem Zusammenhang ist, dass den Lernenden klar wird, wie wichtig die Datenqualität ist. Aktuell arbeiten wir ausschließlich mit hochgeladenen Dateien und setzen das Model Context Protocol noch nicht ein. Die Lernenden erleben also live, wo die Grenzen von generativer KI liegen und wie Daten aufbereitet werden müssen, damit diese in KI-Agenten sauber verarbeitet und dementsprechend qualitative Antworten ausgegeben werden.

So bleibt mir am Ende nur zu sagen: Einfach mal machen und auf das kreative und innovative Potential der Kolleginnen und Kollegen vertrauen. An Hochschulen gibt es viele Freiräume für Experimente. Diese müssen gefunden, erschlossen und genutzt werden.
